reply_text:
The evidence store has about 50 entries mentioning `rowtree` from 10-04, including claude-4's dispatches. Reading them:`rowtree.py` was not created with Write, so it must have come from a Bash heredoc or from a Codex agent. Looking at how the transcripts mention it:The full histories survive in the `.pre-compact-*` snapshots that are kept before each compaction. Replaying across all of them, de-duplicated by tool-call id:The progress page renderer (`progress/render.py`) and `progress.py` have come back, but `rowtree.py` hasn't. It must have been written another way. Searching the tool calls:㊥ (gist) You were right, and it works even better than the Evidence Landscape alone. The evidence entries describe what `rowtree.py` did but don't contain its code. Claude Code's session transcripts do contain the code, and they survived in `/home`. That includes the `.pre-compact-*` snapshots of claude-4's session, which keep its full history. Replaying them has already brought back 17 files from `/tmp/pyreg`, now in `~/recovered-olddisk-tmp/pyreg/`:
- the page renderer, `progress/render.py`, and `SCORECARD.md`
- `overnight/progress.py`, `psweep.py`, `PLAN.md`, `MORNING-2026-10-05.md` and `WHY-NO-CLEAN-ROW-2026-10-06.md`
- the review checklist, the handoff notes and the packets

㊩ (`rowtree.py` is harder) claude-4 never wrote it in one piece. It was created with a shell heredoc at 13:14 on 10-04 and then changed by about 27 small Python patch scripts over the next day. Its data files were built the same way:
- `rowstatus.json`: 33 changes
- `ACCEPTED.tsv`: 65
- `rowmap.py`: 14
- `history.tsv`, which feeds the page: 8
- `deps.tsv`: 7

Every one of those steps is in the transcripts in order, so the files can be rebuilt exactly. But that means replaying the text edits one by one, not running claude-4's old commands, many of which also launched probes. For `history.tsv` there's a shortcut, because the frozen page has every data point in its tooltips.

㊭ (plan)
1. Rebuild these six files by replaying the edits in order, into `mfuton-share/tools/progress/` rather than `/tmp`, and commit them.
2. Check the result against the page: its last snapshot should reproduce "21 CORRECT, 1 COMPILES INCORRECT".
3. Point `render.py` at the new location and bring the page back to life.

It's a self-contained job of about an hour, so I'd normally hand it to a Codex agent and review the result. The raw disk scan can keep running in the background as a cross-check, or I can stop it.

🈸 (go?) Should I dispatch that, or do it myself?

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-11
previous_reply_acts.text: (gist) When a file is deleted, ext4 only marks its blocks as free. The text stays on the disk until something overwrites it. The scan reads the whole old drive, all 2 TB from first byte to last, ignoring the filesystem, and searches for the word `rowtree`. If the deleted `rowtree.py`, or text that mentions it, is still in those freed blocks, the scan records where on the disk each hit is. I can then cut the surrounding bytes out and piece the file back together.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-11
previous_reply_acts.text:
(why it's heavy) It's long rather than costly. 2 TB over USB at about 100 MB/s takes 5–6 hours. So far it has read 60 GB and found nothing yet. The load is small:
- It only reads the old drive, which is read-only anyway.
- It writes almost nothing to the new drive; disk-watch shows no change in writes.
- It runs at idle I/O priority and low CPU priority, so anything else on the box comes first.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-11
previous_reply_acts.text: (whether it's worth it) The odds are modest. The old system ran for a day after the deletion and could have overwritten those blocks. Even a hit may be only a fragment. The fallback is rebuilding `rowtree.py` from the progress page and `PROGRESS-HISTORY.jsonl`, which is maybe an hour's work for an agent. If you'd rather not leave it running, `sudo systemctl stop olddisk-rowtree-scan` ends it and nothing else depends on it.
